entries.title: Israel's election too close to call. And, the Ebola outbreak reaches grim milestone
entries.summary: Israeli voters turned out in record numbers, and the results remain too close to call. And, more than 10,000 people have been infected with Ebola since the outbreak was first declared in May.
entries.content:
Trump Rallies For Republicans, Israel Election Results, Fed Interest Rates Meeting

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Midterm ad spending has surpassed a record $11 billion, according to Ad Impact. An NPR analysis found that candidates in four major Senate races spent more than $15 million on fundraising ads in the 2025-26 election cycle. Meanwhile, President Trump has been campaigning in tight races across states like Texas, Mississippi, and Kansas.

  • 🎧 Trump has not been sticking with his standard midterm pitch, which includes touting GOP tax cuts and attacking Democrats, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First. His jokes, including comments about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted's physique, entertain rally crowds but distract from the key issues the median voter cares about, like the economy and gas prices. Midterm turnout is usually low, but the GOP base still supports him, suggesting many MAGA votes are available, Kurtzleben says. But Trump needing to rally votes in very red states indicates a potential problem for his party.

The election in Israel is too close to call after voters turned out in record numbers to decide whether to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in office or oust him for an alternative. Netanyahu was in a tight race with his top rival Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff. Final vote tallies may take time, and if no bloc secures a majority, it could take days or weeks for party leaders to form a governing coalition and determine the next prime minister.

  • 🎧 Israelis went to bed thinking Eisenkot had the advantage, but by morning, Netanyahu pulled ahead, making the election too close to call, NPR's Daniel Estrin says. Election officials tell NPR that they expect to finish counting votes by tomorrow afternoon. The leading candidate will have six weeks to form a governing coalition, likely competing for support from defectors in each other's camps. Eisenkot could gain the majority of lawmakers' support in parliament, thanks to a strong showing from Arab-led parties eager to see him as prime minister. Eisenkot's camp is hesitant to form a coalition with Arab parties due to mistrust and demonization of Arab political leaders after the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, Estrin says. He adds that both candidates don't have a clear path to a majority coalition.

The Federal Reserve typically combats inflation by raising interest rates. While prices are currently rising faster than average wages, investors don't expect a rate hike at today's meeting.

  • 🎧 The Labor Department's latest cost-of-living report shows consumer prices rose 3.7% in September compared to last year. NPR's Scott Horsley says that marks a larger annual increase than the previous month. Fed policymakers raised interest rates in September, but investors believe the central bank will remain low-key ahead of Election Day and may increase rates again in December.

The Ebola outbreak has surpassed 10,000 people infected since its declaration in May, according to the latest figures from the Democratic Republic of Congo. This outbreak has spread faster than any in history. It is also the largest in geographic scope, spanning from Nigeria to Kenya, and is second in death toll with nearly 5,000 deaths. Around one-third of those who have died have been children.

On the ground

The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.

With Election Day less than a week away, Morning Edition's Michel Martin went to the Midwest to hear from voters about what is important to them this midterm cycle. In Springfield, Ohio, the Trump administration has conducted an aggressive campaign to deport Haitian residents who have been living legally in the country with Temporary Protected Status. The administration revoked TPS for Haitians during Trump's second term. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed has narrowly won the Democratic Senate nomination, a victory for the party's progressive wing. The swing state is important to both parties, which is why Trump and former President Barack Obama campaigned for their party's Senate candidate over the weekend.

Hear what voters in these two states had to say:

  • 🎧 In Michigan, many voters expressed burnout as they worry about gas prices and healthcare.
  • 🎧 Trump's tariffs are hitting Michigan households harder than any other state because many people depend on cross-border trade. But voters affected said the issue isn't so clear-cut.
  • 🎧 Winning a statewide office in Michigan without Detroit is challenging, and El-Sayed didn't perform well there in the primary. Some Black Detroiters said they remain skeptical of him.
  • 🎧 Some Springfield, Ohio voters said they are voting early because they are angry about the administration's treatment of Haitians.

Follow the reporting on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in this newsletter.

The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Life advice

As the holidays approach and appointments and commitments begin to pile up, author Caroline Sylge recommends a "say no" retreat — a day dedicated to figuring out which obligations you want to decline in the coming weeks and months. While it may seem unconventional to devote an entire day to saying no, this approach can help create space for what truly matters to you. Sylge shared with Life Kit her suggested schedule for a "say no" retreat:

  • 🙅 As soon as you wake up, list things you want to say no to. Identify the obvious tasks you want to avoid.
  • 🙅 Take a break, then return to your retreat space and expand your "say no" list. Review requests, appointments, volunteer work and commitments for the coming days, weeks and months. Note the tasks you want to decline, and why.
  • 🙅 After another break, review your list and start saying no. Start with a small win, like crossing off a demanding task. Next, focus on the tougher rejections that may involve saying no to someone you care about or work with.

For more guidance on a "say no" retreat, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

  • The latest installment of Sarah J. Maas' A Court of Thorns and Roses came out on Tuesday, prompting thousands of fans to attend midnight release parties at bookstores nationwide.
  • A federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration's plans to further change East Potomac Park, the municipal D.C. golf course that the president wants to turn into a championship-level venue.
  • Harvard astrophysicists have found what they believe is a previously undiscovered dwarf planet in our solar system. (via WGBH)

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: At least 30 dead in crash between two trains in central Spain, media say
entries.summary: A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 30 people on Wednesday in central Spain, according to local media.
entries.content:
At least 30 dead in crash between two trains in central Spain, media say

BARCELONA, Spain — A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 30 people on Wednesday in central Spain, according to local media.

Spanish authorities initially reported 10 deaths, but Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region, added "that number will surely rise."

Spanish state-owned news agency EFE and other media reported later that the death toll had risen to at least 30.

It was the second major train accident in Spain this year.

Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Padilla told state broadcaster TVE that the accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain. One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track. She said the cause of the crash was not known.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Spanish Health Minister Mónica García told TVE that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.

"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.

The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. It appeared the RENFE train rammed the IRYO train, Spanish media reported. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.

Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.

IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities."

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to injured passengers.

A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police to the crash site.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cancelled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo."

"Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. "All my thoughts are with the victims and their families."

The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, wrote on X that he was on his way to the crash site.

In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

entries.title: Senate candidates built up massive campaign war chests with out-of-state donations
entries.summary: In several competitive U.S. Senate contests, candidates have built healthy campaign accounts with out-of-state donations. But the messages to those donors is very different from the one back at home.
entries.content:
Senate candidates built up massive campaign war chests with out-of-state donations

📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App

In key U.S. Senate races this year, candidates are soliciting donations from outside of their home states, and their out-of-state messaging is different from what they're running locally.

An NPR analysis of Google Ads for four major Senate races — Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas — found that the Democratic and Republican candidates spent more than $15 million on advertising related to fundraising in the 2025-26 election cycle. About three quarters of that went to ads that ran nationally.

Loading...

Often, these ads focus on national talking points — such as attacking or defending President Trump, or turning the Senate blue or red — rather than local issues. For candidates like Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Iowa Democratic nominee Josh Turek, more than 80% of their itemized individual contributions have come from out of state.

Loading...

The funneling of funds has affected at least four of the competitive Senate races, where a majority of the money is coming from outside the state. ActBlue and WinRed, two major grassroots fundraising platforms, are a major catalyst for out-of-state fundraising.

Because this technology is inexpensive to run, it incentivizes candidates to rely on digital ads, according to Zachary Albert, a professor of politics at Brandeis University.

"ActBlue and WinRed really reduced the transaction costs for contributing," Albert said. "Even if you're only yielding like a $5 or $10 contribution from someone like the costs of soliciting that are so much lower than they used to be, that it makes it worthwhile."

With both parties — and each candidate — now having fundraising platforms, political hopefuls increasingly need to stand out from the crowd and are often shifting their messaging to a broader audience, which can result in using polarizing messaging to solicit funds.

Nationalized talking points

For in-state and out-of-state ads, candidates tend to have two different sets of talking points, according to Wesleyan Media Project's Michael Franz.

"In a general election campaign for a [local] TV ad, a candidate will never say, 'I'm the Democrat,' because they want to appeal to moderates and swing voters and they want voters across the aisle," Franz said. "But with a digital ad that's airing outside of your state, the party label becomes more important."

This is reflected in many digital ads. Former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown — who is seeking to regain a place in the Senate — calls to turn his state blue while Georgia Republican Rep. Mike Collins asks people to help turn his state's Senate seat red. Republicans currently control the Senate but there are a number of toss-up races giving Democrats a path to taking back the chamber.

Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson touts her America First credentials in ads for her Senate race, saying she's "America First," while Ossoff in Georgia attacks Trump directly.

According to Michael Heseltine, a researcher at Oxford University who studies how members of congress use social media to communicate, says while there is a large amount of locally-focused messaging, candidates are increasingly spending more time and energy on national talking points.

"[If] we continue on that trend, you'll probably find more and more members who have neglected their constituencies or at least not presented themselves as representatives of their constituencies," he said.

In a statement to NPR, the Ossoff campaign denied targeting audiences by location, and says the campaign "is powered by small-dollar donors because the Senator refuses donations from corporate PACs and federal lobbyists."

The other campaigns declined to comment or did not respond to interview requests.

Daniel Hopkins, a political science professor at the University of Pennsylvania, believes we're in a new era of campaigning, where candidates now have two major stakeholders to appeal to: a voter base which is local, and a donor base which is often larger and nationwide.

"When Jon Ossoff is trying to compete for votes, he's competing against Georgia Republicans," Hopkins said. "But when Jon Ossoff is trying to compete for dollars, he's competing for attention and for donations, ultimately with other prominent Democratic candidates."

The rise of out of state funds

The amount of out-of-state funds for congressional campaigns has been rising each election cycle, according to OpenSecrets.

In order to get these funds, candidates are urged to promote the party platform. Hopkins attributes this to two causes; the party platforms becoming more homogenous and changes in campaign finance laws.

"It used to be that the pathway to success was to rise up through your local party, building the support of local elites in your community," he said.

"The path to political success increasingly goes through a set of, 'ATM districts' around the country that are known to give a lot of money either to Democrats or the Republicans," Hopkins explained.

In states that are dominated by one party, donors might elect to send their funds to a more competitive state to help influence elections, according to Sarah Bryner, a director who studies campaign finance at Public Agenda, a research organization focused on democracy.

"People from California really don't feel like they have much to do because their state's going to go blue regardless," she said. "So they support candidates in states like Georgia or Texas."

Democrats took the lead, but Republicans are catching up

While both parties now benefit from out-of-state funds, Democrats tended to rely on them, due to weaker local funding systems in competitive states like Ohio and Michigan. As a result, Democrats built a system for grassroots donations — ActBlue which launched in 2004 — nearly 15 years before Republicans, who launched WinRed in 2019.

While some of the Democratic advantage in out-of-state fundraising can be attributed to Republican incumbents' connections to local funding, part of it can be attributed to the Democratic Party's diverse base of voters.

"You're having to bring together that diverse coalition, not necessarily around some unified ideological agenda, but based on a kind of discrete policy [that] claims to represent particular groups," said Brandeis University's Zachary Albert.

Meanwhile, Republicans were initially slow to realize the potential for small dollar fundraising until Trump.

"The Republicans realized, especially during Trump, that they do have a national audience of small donors ready to activate behind their preferred candidates for their preferred agenda," Public Agenda's Sarah Bryner said.

Looking forward

While some states are trying to limit outside funds, like Hawaii implementing a cap on out-of-state donations starting in 2027, it's difficult to regulate at a national level, according to University of Massachusetts political science professor Raymond La Raja.

"It's going to be hard to do constitutionally, especially because the Supreme Court has ruled you can't prevent groups from spending as much money as they want in elections," he said.

In June, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of coordinated campaign spending which allows more out of state funds to be spent in elections. So far, the National Republican Senatorial Committee has spent three times as much on advertisements at this point than in the previous midterms.

La Raja suggested fund matching, where local donations would be matched with public funds, using New York City as a model. He believes this would shift candidates to focus more on their constituents' issues rather than national ones.

Bryner mentioned the Alaska top donor disclosure law as an option to localize fundraising. There, ads have to list the top three donors. Colorado and Virginia have similar laws for online and broadcast ads.

While funding can influence how a candidate talks about their race locally and nationally, Bryner isn't convinced this will completely tip the scale of elections. Candidates who've outraised with out-of-state funds, like Amy McGrath, who ran against Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell in Kentucky and Beto O'Rourke against Republican Sen. Ted Cruz in Texas, often lose against their opponents. She advises against appealing to donors out-of-state because ultimately it doesn't translate into votes.

"As much as money in politics is such a factor in America, voters are still ultimately who makes the final decision" Bryner said. "And if you're getting all your money from outside of the state, those people can't vote for you."

entries.title: Why many student voters have a right to choose where to register to vote
entries.summary: Student voters studying outside their hometown have a right to choose where they register to vote. Advocates say a Montana legal fight is a reminder of a misunderstanding of those students' rights.
entries.content:
Why many student voters have a right to choose where to register to vote

Many student voters studying outside their hometown face a key decision before they even get a ballot: Should they register to vote where they go to school?

A Supreme Court ruling in 1979 affirmed the right of eligible students to register in the communities where they live during the academic year. But close to a half-century later, some people continue to question why students can vote in their college towns.

That issue resurfaced in discussions about changes Montana made last year to its requirements for residents who want to register to vote. After a student advocacy group sued, a state judge blocked the new restriction for now. That leaves the previous rules in place for Montana students who want to register to vote, including for the midterm elections through Election Day.

Now, as the wait continues for the judge's final ruling, some experts on student voting see the case as a reminder of common misunderstandings about the rights of some of the country's youngest voters.

Why out-of-state college students are like owners of multiple homes

Voting in the U.S. is tied to residency, and state and local governments determine who qualifies as a resident who can register.

To make sure certain voters, such as eligible students, are not discriminated against, federal law sets ground rules for residency requirements, explains Michael Hanmer, a professor of government and politics at the University of Maryland, whose research has focused on student voters.

"You can't apply different standards to different groups of people, so college students need to be treated the same as anybody else in the mix here who might be new to a particular place," Hanmer says.

All eligible voters have a right to cast a ballot somewhere. And like owners of multiple homes, many students are able to choose which of their residences to be that somewhere for registering to vote. In the legal world, it's known as their "domicile."

"It's defined as the one singular, fixed, permanent, principal home where one intends to return, although she may not currently reside there," explains Yael Bromberg, an attorney who co-edited the book Youth Voting Rights: Civil Rights, the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, and the Fight for American Democracy on College Campuses. "In the case of a student who may not know where she might live after graduation, that determination of domicile is highly personal and an individualized assessment."

How Montana's new law could stop thousands of eligible students from voting

In Montana, a U.S. citizen who is 18 or older and has been a state resident for at least 30 days is generally eligible to register to vote there.

Last year, Montana's Republican-controlled legislature passed a new restriction for "temporary" residents in an "educational program." Under the revised state law, they could only register in a Montana county if they intend to make the county or the state their permanent home at the end of their program.

GOP state officials argue that restriction does not apply to students at colleges and universities in Montana. That interpretation, they claim in a court filing, "would render the word 'temporary' meaningless, because no one understands obtaining a two, four, or eight-year degree as a temporary endeavor."

So far, Missoula County Judge Jason Marks is not buying that argument. In February, he found the restriction against student voters likely violates Montana's constitution.

After holding a hearing this month, Marks is now preparing his final ruling for the lawsuit brought by student advocates at the Montana Public Interest Research Group. MontPIRG claims the change to Montana's residency rule could force thousands of students to lose the ability to have a say at the ballot box about how their communities are run.

Why out-of-state student voters should be aware of other state requirements

At a public hearing last year, some of the restriction's supporters said student voters from outside Montana should not be able to affect the state's elections.

But Hanmer at the University of Maryland doesn't see Montana's law clearing legal hurdles.

"I would be surprised if this attempt to restrict students from voting if they're in Montana just for educational purposes holds up," he says.

Still, Hanmer points out student voters who do have the right to choose where to register should keep in mind that, in some states, that choice may come with other requirements.

"If they want to follow through and vote in that new state, then they might have to engage in some additional activities that could be costly in terms of their time," Hanmer says. Certain states require a new resident to, for example, get a new state ID or change their car registration. "They can impose these restrictions," Hanmer adds, "but they impose them on all new residents, not just college students."

Edited by Benjamin Swasey

entries.title: Partnerships between ICE and local police surge, report finds
entries.summary: The number of state and local officers working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement has doubled in size in the last eight months, according to a new report from the immigration reform advocacy group FWD.us.
entries.content:
Partnerships between ICE and local police surge, report finds

The number of state and local officers working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement has doubled in size in the last eight months, according to a new report from the immigration reform advocacy group FWD.us.

The group analyzed the federal ICE program, called 287(g), that deputizes state and local police for immigration enforcement. It used the agency's public records and information requested by the Deportation Data Project, which is based at UC Berkeley and UCLA and collects U.S. immigration enforcement data.

More than 29,000 officers were deputized by ICE between January 2025 and October 2026. That's far more than the 11,600 deportation officers directly employed by ICE.

Felicity Rose, vice president of research and policy at FWRD, says her organization's analysis highlights just how big a role these partnerships have played in the Trump administration's immigration enforcement work. The program was created in the 1990s under the Clinton administration but was little used — until President Trump returned to office.

"These state and local officers are a key lever in the administration's quieter approach to enforcement. They're trading what used to be splashy urban surges, which we saw in Chicago and Minneapolis, for just routine highway stops now under the 287(g) program," Rose told NPR ahead of the report's release.

The most common and most aggressive form of these 287(g) partnerships, the Task Force Model, allows police and sheriff's departments to make immigration arrests. And, in return, as long as these local agencies remain in "active and ongoing participation in 287(g) enforcement activity outlined" in the agreements signed with ICE , they get money to spend on new cars, equipment and other enforcement resources.

The Department of Homeland Security has said that 287(g) is a critical tool to cut down on crime and illegal immigration.

A more granular look

Law enforcement agencies in Florida and Texas, combined, accounted for about half of the more than 47,000 immigration arrests made nationally between January 2025 and August 2026 through 287(g), FWRD found.

That is not such a surprise — governors in both of those states have mandated local police sign these deals. And aggressive enforcement by state and local police in Florida and Texas has made headlines.

Some states not usually known for aggressive enforcement also recorded a spike in immigration arrests made by deputized officers.

The FWD.us report showed that 287(g)-certified officers in Wyoming, New Hampshire and Oklahoma were responsible for huge shares of immigration arrests in each state in recent months.

In Wyoming, deputized officers made 77% of the total immigration arrests in the state in April 2026 and more than 60% every month since November 2025, the report found. Similarly, in New Hampshire, the program was responsible for 60% of immigration arrests there in June 2026.

In June, close to 50% of immigration arrests in Oklahoma were made by state or local police.

Oklahoma's Highway Patrol signed all of its troopers on to 287(g), giving their officers the power to stop a driver and potentially make an immigration arrest on state highways.

That has had a chilling effect on immigrant communities living in the state according to Gabriela Ramirez-Perez, the immigration and economic security policy analyst with the Oklahoma Policy Institute, a think tank that analyzes state policy.

"Even though Oklahoma may not be in the headlines, it's definitely a hotspot for immigration enforcement," Ramirez-Perez said. "We can say that it's definitely resulting in a lot of fear in immigrant communities. People are changing their day to day routines to try to avoid getting on the highway, to try to avoid driving as much as possible."

Financial incentives

The Justice Department earlier this summer offered $3 billion in funding for state and local agencies that join the program. The money can go toward staffing and new equipment in the coming years.

Florida has already given hundreds of millions of additional money to law enforcement agencies in the state in exchange for their participation in the program.

Rose, with FWRD, says the promise of money appears to be a driving force behind the surge in 287(g) participation, and thinks it will lead to more partnerships in the future.

entries.title: Here's how Democrats in Congress are preparing for election fraud claims
entries.summary: Congressional Democrats are working with good governance groups to create an action plan for any potential claims of election fraud.
entries.content:
Here's how Democrats in Congress are preparing for election fraud claims

Congressional Democrats are forming a task force to protect election results

This story has been updated from a story first reported in August.

This midterm cycle, the Trump administration has gathered millions of state voter records for law enforcement purposes, endeavored to restrict mail-in voting nationwide, declined the typical practice of inviting international election observers and repeatedly raised the idea of dispatching armed federal personnel to  voting locations.

The Trump administration broadly describes its actions as an effort to ensure the integrity of the American democratic system after the president's signature election overhaul effort, the SAVE America Act, foundered in the GOP-led Senate.

In a statement to NPR in October, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said that "President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections. While extreme Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump Administration is taking decisive action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion."

This summer, NPR spoke to more than a dozen people who've formed what they describe as an election protection task force. It's a coordinated effort between Democratic lawmakers and their staffers, election litigators, scholars and nonpartisan good governance organizations.

Those involved worry that the administration will point to normal, but poorly understood, parts of American election infrastructure, including slow vote counting in California and Alaska, as evidence of fraudulent behavior. They also say that the administration has long worked to undermine public trust in a secure and transparent election system and has, without constitutional authority, inserted the executive branch into the state-led election process.

Democracy Forward — a legal nonprofit that says it works to advance democracy and social progress through litigation, policy and public education — has written that the Trump administration's efforts "harness the president's longstanding and baseless conspiracy theories in pursuit of discovering so-called 'election fraud.' These actions are reckless and run the risk of intimidating and disenfranchising voters."

Even as task force members acknowledged there is no magic "protect democracy" button tucked away in a Capitol cloakroom, they each emphasized the power of legislators as messengers and organizers. Their primary goal is to to prepare the public and their state and local counterparts to act when necessary to ensure election results are honored.

Establishing the midterm narrative

"We have very important elections coming up," Trump said in a July address from the East Room of the White House. "We want those elections to be honest."

He used the speech to call on Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would, among other measures, require voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote and a photo ID before they can cast a ballot.

"How easy is that to do, unless you want to cheat? The only reason you wouldn't do it is you want to cheat because your policies are so bad, and your candidates are so pathetic that you can't get away or can't get elected any other way," he said.

Members of the Democratic task force said the remarks should be understood as an effort to make voter fraud — which studies and investigations have found to be vanishingly rare — seem plausible.

Justin Vail, a leader at Protect Democracy, a cross-ideological group that says it uses litigation, advocacy and research to protect American elections is a member of the task force. He previously served as a special assistant to President Joe Biden, working on democracy issues. He told NPR that Trump's speech was an effort to sow doubt in November's elections, a first step in what his organization characterizes as a three-step playbook: deceive, disrupt and deny.

"First, he deceives Americans, manufacturing false claims about voter fraud and the security of our elections," Vail said. "Second, he seeks to disrupt the normal state and local management of elections," he continued, "in an attempt to coerce them to enact policies that threaten the eligible voters' access. And if that's all not enough, Trump is prepared to outright deny election results that he doesn't like."

The fight in courts

Marc Elias, the prominent election litigator and a member of the task force, describes the election protection effort on a continuum.

"It begins with voter registration, then you have people voting, then you have Election Day," Elias said. "You have tabulation of ballots, you have local certification, and ultimately you have seating."

"History has shown that Donald Trump is willing to weaponize power against all points of that process," Elias said. "This is not something that we wait until election subversion has taken place."

Elias' firm has been at the leading edge of election-related litigation against the administration. He said his team has been combating what he views as the first stage of an ongoing election interference effort. They have been involved in dozens of lawsuits spanning every state.

A primary fight centered on mail-in ballots. Trump ordered the Postal Service to deliver mail-in ballots only to registered voters on those lists — an effort that was ultimately halted by the Supreme Court.

The Department of Homeland Security has also worked for months to gather state voter rolls, which it says it is using to find noncitizens who are illegally registered to vote.

A tally by the State Democracy Research Initiative at the University of Wisconsin-Madison has tallied 31 federal lawsuits from the administration seeking state voter data. States have largely refused to comply, citing privacy laws and the Constitution, which expressly delegates election administration to the states subject to congressional oversight.

Common Cause, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization, challenged the Justice Department's voter data collection program as violating federal law in court. On October 9, 2026, a federal district court ruled that the policy exceeds the Justice Department's authority, is arbitrary and capricious, and violates federal law.

The court vacated the policy nationwide, impacting not only the Justice Department's efforts to get data from the states that have resisted as well as states that had already voluntarily complied. The Justice Department has appealed the decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

The limits of Congress

Limited in their ability to exercise hard power, Democratic lawmakers have exercised power in other ways. Primarily, elected Democrats are focused on being the connective tissue between their state and local counterparts involved in the mechanics of administering elections and the good governance groups involved in ensuring the integrity of that process.

"We recognize that elections are run at the local level, at the state level, and we want to be able to partner — and continue to partner — with our state authorities as they carry out their duties," said Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, D-Del., told NPR in August.

"But we also know that, especially at this moment, there are civil society organizations, there are attorneys, there are community leaders who are all coming together and saying we're each going to do our part to ensure that this election is safe, reliable, strong, that workers at the polls are protected, that our voters can get out there and vote," she said.

Still, Elias believes Congress could play a larger role in protecting elections if it was able to speak with a unified, bipartisan voice, but "it's not doing that because Mike Johnson and John Thune aren't doing it," he said, referring to the top Republicans in the House and Senate, respectively.

"Imagine," Elias said, "a brief that was submitted by the House of Representatives itself, the U.S. Senate itself, telling the courts that Congress was jealously guarding its authority" over elections. "That, I think, would frankly be an incredibly useful thing and would have a real impact."

GOP legislators broadly echo the president's election fraud narratives, and leaders have shown little desire to push back on his election-related actions. Congressional Republicans have instead focused much of their attention on trying to pass the SAVE America Act.

Despite their minority status, Democrats do have access to some oversight tools. While the House of Representatives has an active staff election observer program that dates to the 1980s, this year will see the first-ever Senate election observer program.

Staff designated by lawmakers of both parties can be dispatched to observe voting and tabulating locations, with the goal of keeping lawmakers informed for oversight work and in case of contested results. Those who volunteer to participate will not advocate for candidates, participate in vote counting or interfere with voters or election staff.

"I am committed to using every tool to protect free and fair elections, and the new Senate Election Observer Program will do just that," Padilla, the top Democrat on the Senate committee that oversees election administration, said in a statement announcing the program.

Senate Democratic Majority Leader Schumer and Padilla announced this month that more than 100 staff had agreed to participate. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., who chairs the committee, has not addressed whether Republican staffers would participate.

What comes next

Some members of the task force are now prepared for worst-case scenarios with prewritten legal briefs and a Rolodex of key contacts in places they believe to be high risk. Their lists include areas in which election officials may have echoed the president's election denial rhetoric, where results are expected to be close or slow to count, and where Trump has focused scrutiny in the past, like California, Illinois and New York.

Several members noted that over the last year, Trump has attempted to dramatically expand direct federal involvement in elections and asserted unprecedented authority over election administration.

"Remember, the States are merely an 'agent' for the Federal Government in counting and tabulating the votes," he wrote on Truth Social last August. "They must do what the Federal Government, as represented by the President of the United States, tells them, FOR THE GOOD OF OUR COUNTRY, to do."

Multiple election law experts consulted for this story, none of whom are involved in advising congressional lawmakers or candidates, broadly agreed that the president has no role in election administration, which the Constitution delegates explicitly to the states and Congress.

Despite the risks they see, many of those involved in congressional Democrats' election preparations felt optimistic that, in the end, the voice of the American public would win out.

Vanita Gupta, formerly Biden's associate attorney general and now director of the Center for Law and Public Trust at New York University's law school, is among those optimistic voices.

"Hundreds of nonpartisan organizations have been preparing over the past year to do everything in our power to protect the integrity of our elections," Gupta told NPR in August. "Maybe the process of getting from here to a new Congress may be messier than any of us would like, perhaps filled with a lot more litigation and organizing than we might have thought was necessary, but we are going to have free and fair elections so long as people don't take for granted their right to vote."

entries.title: Are you an organ donor? Here are some rule changes you may want to know
entries.summary: Transplant teams can talk to families about organ donation before they've decided whether to continue life-sustaining medical care for loved ones. Until now, that has been forbidden.
entries.content:
Organ donation conversations are changing. Critics worry families may feel pressured

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

The U.S. organ transplant system is making a controversial change to a long-standing rule that was designed to protect potential donors. The revision aims to boost donations and reduce errors. But critics worry that the move may endanger patient care.

Under the change, the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network, which runs the transplant system, will relax a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital and the transplantation team standing by to procure patients' organs.

Previously, no one from that team was even supposed to talk to family members until after they had made the heart-wrenching decision to let a loved one go. The rule was intended to prevent pressure that could change the care patients receive. It was also in place to dispel any doubts that doctors aren't doing everything they can to save patients.

But the board of directors for the transplant system voted Aug. 20 to modify that rule as part of a new set of guidelines governing donation following circulatory death. That occurs after life-sustaining care has been withdrawn and now accounts for about half of organ donations.

The new rules, which go into effect Nov. 18, "allow discussions for organ donation to take place once end of life discussions are taking place with the potential deceased donor's agent," according to the new policy.

Why is the firewall previously barring these conversations coming down?

"I think the best way to think about it is that insisting on a bright line without focusing on what's happening on either side of that line is a false sense of security," Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ network, told NPR in an interview.

The new rules aim to prevent disturbing mistakes that have occurred in the past. Those errors have included patients being wheeled into operating rooms to remove their organs when they were still alive.

"That specific line in the policy is part of a suite of improvements to the coordination and communication between the organ procurement organizations and the healthcare team that is caring for these patients in hospitals and the families of the patients themselves. And that really is a marked improvement over the policy that was in place before," Lynch says.

A balance of safety and speed

In addition to allowing donation teams to approach families sooner, the new policies include making it easier to pause organ retrieval if anyone becomes concerned that something is amiss and standardizing other patient protections, including testing for determining death.

"Documentation, clear coordination, deference to the primary healthcare team and consequences — that's what keeps patients safe," says Lynch.

The change in policy is also designed to make sure the organ retrieval team isn't brought in too late to conduct the tests and preparation necessary for families to honor their loved one's desire to be a donor.

When that happens, "the family loses out on that memory" of helping their loved one donate their organs, "the patient loses out on the choice that they made, and the people on the waiting list lose out on the chance to receive a lifesaving organ," Lynch says.

More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to the Health Resources & Services Administration. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.

Does the change cross an ethical line?

Critics, however, say the change is dangerous. It could subtly pressure families and caregivers to discontinue care and create confusion about who's in the intensive care unit to try to save their loved one and who's there to obtain their organs, which could deepen distrust in the organ donation system.

"It's a very important bright line," says Dr. Lainie Ross, a bioethicist at the University of Rochester. "Our primary responsibility is that patient's well-being and care. And we need a bright line. That's where our focus is, and we're not even going to start thinking about whether those organs are usable until death is inevitable and imminent."

She adds: "When my family member is in that hospital bed, I want to know that we're all on Team Mom and not worried the reason the doctor's really suggesting the treatments aren't working is because they want your organs for someone else."

Ross says she's "horrified to think that families will feel pressured. They'll feel manipulated."

Others also see problems with the change.

"I don't disagree with the desire to have more transplantable organs. I think transplants provide great benefit to many, many people," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network's Patient Affairs Committee. "But people may be pressured to make that decision too quickly. I don't want to interfere with a family's grieving process, and I don't want to interfere with a family's ability to make a decision for their family member at a time when it's correct for them."

Some critics say the change is the latest worrisome development for organ donors.

"This is part of a number of things that are going on in organ donation that are blurring lines," says Lois Shepherd, a professor of law and bioethics at the University of Virginia who opposed the change as a member of the working group that developed the new guidelines. "A lot of safeguards for patients are weakening. And that's a concern to me."

But the change was endorsed by the Association of Organ Procurement Organizations (AOPO), a trade group.

"Families/agents who are considering [withdrawing life support] must be informed about donation and how the donor evaluation process may affect the timing of the [withdrawal of life support]," the group said in its public comments. "Many families have expressed frustration with learning about this timing impact after planning for other family members to be present at the time of [withdrawing life support]. Waiting until the family has made the decision is too late."

The AOPO declined to make someone available for an interview with NPR. But AOPO President Allison Erickson said in a written statement: "Donation depends on public trust, and it is our responsibility to respect and maintain it. Any time there is confusion or concern, [organ procurement organizations] clarify and improve the process. Donor families deserve to fully understand each stage of the end-of-life and donation processes, as well as that their loved ones are cared for by all involved."

entries.title: How a lifelong Republican came to lead the data center battle in Ohio
entries.summary: In Ohio, many people are displeased with the state's rapid buildout of data centers. It's a hot issue in the midterms, as political candidates from both parties try to ease voter concerns.
entries.content:
How a lifelong Republican came to lead the data center battle in Ohio

Candidates work to ease concerns as data centers become hot-button issue for Ohioans

Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.

MT. ORAB, Ohio — The data center mystery in this rural exurb of Cincinnati has consumed Nick Owens.

The lifelong Republican and self-described small-town attorney has spent countless hours trying to figure out what's going on with 1,000 acres of farmland and trees that property records show were sold to a data center developer in 2024 and 2025.

In a few spots, the data center property runs right up against beautiful two-story homes.

"This is the Ohio that people brag about. This is the Ohio people love. This is the small town charm," he says. "Living in the rural area, but getting the benefits of a nice, lovely neighborhood."

Some of the most coordinated opposition to data centers anywhere in the country grew out of what happened in secrecy in this village of 4,300 people, a short drive up a country road from Owens' home.

Nondisclosure agreements have stymied Owens' efforts to learn more. But along his quest, he crossed paths with another local attorney and a real estate agent who were equally alarmed. Together, they mobilized a network of volunteers in nearly all 88 counties in the state. They are Democrats, Republicans and Independents. They called themselves Conserve Ohio.

"We all share the same ethos and the same passion for preserving our way of life, preserving the future of Ohio, frankly, from the hyperscale data center invasion," says Owens. "It's really beautiful."

This fall, the group is behind ballot initiatives in 10 communities that would amend local charters to prohibit the construction of large-scale data centers — the kind used to power artificial intelligence. It's an effort that goes beyond the temporary pauses that hundreds of municipal and county governments have embraced.

"All too often you hear from the politicians, 'Well, the community should have a say,'" says Owens. "We're going to find out in ten communities whether or not the communities want them."

Meanwhile, the grassroots group is working on a more ambitious undertaking: a petition for an amendment to the state constitution that would ban large-scale data centers statewide. Their goal is to put that to Ohio's voters in 2027.

Data centers bring economic benefits and angst

It's been more than a decade since tech companies first came to Ohio, drawn by the state's inexpensive and abundant land, its energy infrastructure and its generous tax breaks. That combination paved the way for some of the fastest data center growth in the country.

Now, despite the economic benefits — considerable tax revenue, money for schools, numerous construction jobs and a smaller number of permanent jobs — no one seems to want a computing campus in their backyard, especially one shrouded in secrecy.

"Should the school have extra money or the local government have extra money so we have a constant hum and ridiculous amounts of emissions and pollution?" Owens says, pointing out that hyperscale data centers will require new power plants. "Our community is not for sale."

Pressed to consider whether the state should forgo all opportunities, Owens says he'd entertain the idea of putting data centers on old industrial sites, where they'd be buffered from people.

"If we're going to have data centers, those are the prime places," he says, while acknowledging that it'd be cheaper and easier for a developer to build on pristine farmland than on an old coal site. "I don't know if there are enough brownfield sites, but shouldn't we start with those first?"

A hot-button election issue

In recent months, candidates running for statewide office in Ohio have been trying to convince voters that they hear their concerns — even as they stop short of backing the kind of sweeping moratorium data center opponents are seeking.

Until recently, data center projects weren't all that controversial, in part because they were smaller and weren't being built for AI.

But as the issue has gained traction, it's become a hot topic in the midterms, including in the tight race to fill a U.S. Senate seat. Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown has cast his opponent, the incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, as "the face of data centers." Brown has been reminding voters that as lieutenant governor, Husted welcomed tech companies to Ohio and championed their data center investments.

Meanwhile, Husted has accused Brown of hypocrisy, pointing to Brown's past support for data centers.

Husted has also introduced his own solution, pushing a bill in Congress aimed at getting data centers to pay for power grid upgrades and other costs associated with their massive energy use. Senate Democrats have blocked the bill, calling it toothless, prompting Husted to accuse the Democrats of not caring or helping.

Unconvinced that politicians will help

These political gestures have not persuaded Linda Moodie, an independent who's been volunteering with Conserve Ohio. She doesn't trust that any of the candidates running for statewide office "will do the right thing" if elected, which is to give the people a say in the data center buildout.

"It's really something that I think a lot of us didn't see coming, and all of a sudden there's just an influx of them," she says.

Between now and election day, she's seizing every opportunity to collect signatures to get the statewide ban on the ballot next year.

On a recent evening, she set up a booth at the "Halloween on the Green" celebration in the Cincinnati suburb of Fairfield. She handed out candy to kids and clipboards with the petition to parents. Both were enthusiastically received.

"The closer it hits to home, the more people that are going to want to do something," says Moodie.

A dampening of voter enthusiasm in a Republican stronghold

Two years ago, Owens served as a Trump delegate at the Republican National Convention. He won't say how he's voting this fall, but he says no doubt the data center issue, along with $6 diesel, have dampened Republican enthusiasm.

Throughout Mt. Orab, the absence of campaign yard signs is notable.

"Two years ago you would have seen Donald Trump signs left and right," says Owens.

This county, like much of rural Ohio, voted 80% for President Trump in 2024.

"You always have depressed votes in the midterms," says Owens. "But I think the enthusiasm gap for Republicans in particularly rural areas is going to be a lot more pronounced… than any type of enthusiasm gap for Democrats in the cities."

Trump's belittling of data center opponents isn't helping, he says, citing recent comments the president posted to his social media platform Truth Social.

"The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump wrote. "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame."

Owens calls the president's statements "tone deaf."

"I mean, no one wants to be poor or backwards," he says. "I want our regular way of life."

Construction at the Mt. Orab site hasn't yet begun. It's not clear when it will. Owens says because of nondisclosure agreements, people who live here know nothing.

For now, standing at the edge of the data center property on a crisp fall day, it's nearly silent but for the birds.

entries.title: New teachers union president wants to steer educators away from partisan politics
entries.summary: NEA President Princess Moss wants to move her organization, the nation's largest labor union, toward issue-based advocacy — and away from party politics.
entries.content:
New teachers union president wants to steer educators away from partisan politics

The public education landscape is a bit of a minefield these days.

Inflation is blowing up school budgets. A new education tax credit that will direct federal tax dollars into private schools goes into effect in January. At the same time, the Trump administration is dismantling the Department of Education brick by brick.

Enter Princess Moss, the new face of the nation's largest labor union, the National Education Association. Its membership includes 3 million teachers and public workers from every state.

"Public education is under attack," she says. "Our students are under attack. The very foundation of this democracy is public education — that is under attack."

Her vision for the NEA — what she calls "resistance to renaissance" — has some markings of past leadership. It puts things like professional autonomy and community organizing front and center, but there is one stark departure she wants for the union.

"I want us to become our own political authority," Moss says. "Meaning that we're not aligning ourselves with a political party."

"I know this can work because I've done it before"

Princess Moss grew up the daughter of two school bus drivers in Spotsylvania County in rural Virginia. She recalls many teachers from her childhood who inspired her to pursue a career in schools. But her second grade teacher, Lucy T. Lewis, stands out. Moss remembers Lewis telling her she was smart back in 1968, even after she misspelled the word refrigerator in front of the entire class.

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

"I wanted to be just like Mrs. Lewis," she says. "Where you could help students learn and help students be the best that they could be even if they made a mistake every now and then."

Moss went on to work as an elementary school music teacher for more than 20 years in a neighboring county. Along the way she rose up the ranks in state union leadership, presiding over the Virginia Education Association from 2004 to 2008 and eventually moving up the ladder at the NEA. Moss now takes on the challenge of navigating a difficult political climate over her three-year term as president.

"We are the experts," she says. "We want to be at the decision-making tables."

One lesson she brings from her time in Virginia is that when she focused on the issues, there were allies to be found in unexpected places.

At the time, Virginia had a Democratic governor and Republican-controlled general assembly. She worked on building coalitions across the aisle and emphasized that public education is for everyone. With the midterms rapidly approaching, Moss said she's bringing that mentality to the NEA.

"Talk about your students"

"We're telling our members: 'Talk about your students. What do your students need?'" she says. "Don't make it a Democrat or Republican issue."

Michael Petrilli, the president of the right-leaning think tank the Fordham Institute, isn't quite so convinced: "Look, that would be a huge departure for the NEA," he says. "They have been stalwart supporters of the Democratic Party and vice versa."

In 2020, the NEA recommended Joe Biden for the office and in 2024 issued a formal endorsement for Vice President Kamala Harris.

Petrilli has long held reservations about the nation's teachers unions, saying their positions often block meaningful changes to teaching and perpetuate strict salary rules that can make it hard to recruit and fill certain jobs. But he says he's open to seeing where things go this year, especially with many state-level races leaning in the direction of the union's longtime allies — Democrats.

"This is going to put the unions in a very good position to be able to drive education policy," he says. "I think this is the question: What are they going to do with that power? What are they going to push these Democratic governors to get done?"

Even with Democrats favored to win some races and continued criticism of the union from some Republicans, Moss says she's focused on building a broad coalition of support for public schools.

"The bottom line is that we will work with those who want to put public education first," she says. "No matter what the political party, no matter what your inclination."

Edited by Nirvi Shah

Audio story produced by Lauren Migaki
